title: Transistor Circuits
description: Switches, followers, current sources and common-emitter amplifiers with H&H's simple transistor model.

study.title: First transistor model
study.body: For an npn transistor: the collector is more positive than the emitter; the base–emitter junction conducts like a diode, so $V_B \approx V_E + 0.6$ V, while the base–collector junction is reverse biased; and every maximum rating is respected. Then the collector current is $h_{FE}$ times the base current. $h_{FE}$ (β) is roughly 100 but varies from about 50 to 250 between specimens of one type and with current and temperature. **A circuit that depends on an exact β is a bad circuit.** H&H rounds $V_{BE}$ to 0.6 V (the semiconductors unit used 0.7 V); both are just estimates, and a good design works with either.

study.title: The transistor switch
study.body: When the input goes high, $I_C = h_{FE}I_B$ asks for more collector current than the load allows, so the transistor **saturates**: $V_{CE(sat)} \approx$ 0.05–0.2 V and the load gets nearly the full supply. Give about **10× the minimum base current**: $h_{FE}$ drops at low $V_{CE}$, and a cold lamp draws 5–10× its rated current. $R_2$ keeps the base at ground when the input floats. An inductive load (relay, motor) needs a **flyback diode** $D_1$, otherwise the coil drives the collector far above $V_{CC}$ at switch-off.

study.title: Emitter follower
study.body: The emitter follows the base one diode drop lower: no voltage gain, but current (and power) gain. A load at the emitter looks $h_{FE}+1$ times larger from the base (formula), and a source resistance looks $h_{FE}+1$ times smaller from the emitter: $R_{out} \approx R_s/(h_{FE}+1)$. That makes the follower the standard **buffer** between a high-impedance source and a low-impedance load. Rule of thumb: make each output impedance ≤ 1/10 of the input impedance it drives.

study.title: Biasing a follower
study.body: With an ac-coupled input on a single supply, a divider sets the quiescent point. For the largest symmetric swing put $V_E = V_{CC}/2$, pick $R_E$ for the quiescent current and set $V_B = V_E + 0.6$. Make the divider **stiff**, $R_1 \| R_2 \lesssim \frac{1}{10}h_{FE}R_E$, so $V_B$ hardly depends on $h_{FE}$. $C_1$ and the input resistance form a high-pass filter, $f_{3dB} = 1/(2\pi R_{in}C_1)$, below the lowest signal frequency. With ± supplies and a signal near ground no divider or capacitors are needed, but the base still needs a dc path to ground.

study.title: Transistor current source
study.body: Hold the base at a fixed $V_B$: the emitter sits at $V_B - 0.6$, so $R_E$ fixes the emitter current, and the collector current is almost the same whatever the load. This works while the transistor stays active, so the collector may range from about $V_E + 0.2$ V up to the supply: the **compliance** range. Choose $V_E \gtrsim 1$ V so that $V_{BE}$ changes of a few tens of mV (temperature, Early effect) hardly change the current.

study.title: Common-emitter amplifier
study.body: A current source with a resistor as load: a base wiggle $v_{in}$ reappears at the emitter, gives $i_c \approx v_{in}/R_E$, and $R_C$ turns that into $v_{out} = -i_cR_C$. Transconductance view: $g_m = 1/R_E$. Bias the collector near $V_{CC}/2$ for the largest symmetric swing. $R_{in} = R_1 \| R_2 \| h_{FE}R_E$, $R_{out} \approx R_C$. With $R_C = R_E$ and $V_C \approx 0.75V_{CC}$ it is a unity-gain **phase splitter** (outputs at collector and emitter).

study.title: Explore: follower clipping
study.body: A ±15 V follower with $R_E$ = 1.5 kΩ to −15 V (10 mA quiescent) drives a load $R_L$ to ground, output resting at 0 V. On negative half-cycles the load must be fed through $R_E$ only; once the transistor cuts off, the output is just the divider $-V_{EE}R_L/(R_L + R_E)$. Make $R_L$ small and watch the negative peaks flatten while the positive ones stay clean.

steps.title: A transistor in four rules
steps.body: H&H's first model of an npn: the collector is more positive than the emitter, the base–emitter junction conducts like a diode ($V_{BE} \approx 0.6$ V), the base–collector junction is reverse biased, and then $I_C = h_{FE}I_B$. Think of the collector as a current controlled by the base, not as a resistor.

steps.prompt: In a working circuit you measure an npn with $V_B$ = 3.0 V and $V_E$ = 1.2 V. That is a normal operating condition.
steps.explanation: A conducting base–emitter junction clamps $V_{BE}$ at about 0.6–0.7 V. Here $V_{BE}$ = 3.0 − 1.2 = 1.8 V, which a healthy, conducting junction cannot sustain. Most likely the B–E junction has failed open (or you are probing the wrong pins). Checking $V_{BE}$ is a classic first step in debugging.

steps.prompt: An npn has its base held at $V_B$ = {{VB|V}} and a resistor $R_E$ = {{RE|Ω}} from emitter to ground. The collector goes to +15 V through a small load. Assume $h_{FE}$ is large.

ask.explanation: $V_E = V_B - 0.6$ = {{VB-0.6|V}}, so $I_E = V_E/R_E$ = {{VB-0.6|V}} / {{RE|Ω}} = {{(VB-0.6)/RE|A}}. With large $h_{FE}$, $I_C \approx I_E$ = **{{(VB-0.6)/RE|A}}**, whatever the exact $h_{FE}$.

steps.title: The transistor switch
steps.body: Here a logic signal switches a relay coil. When the transistor is driven hard enough it **saturates** ($V_{CE} \approx$ 0.05–0.2 V) and the coil sees almost the full $V_{CC}$. Design rules: provide about 10× the base current that $I_C/h_{FE(min)}$ would suggest, put a resistor from base to ground, and put a flyback diode across any inductive load.

steps.prompt: A {{Vin|V}} logic output switches a relay coil of {{Rc|Ω}} from $V_{CC}$ = {{VCC|V}} through an npn with $h_{FE(min)}$ = {{hFE}}. Choose $R_B$ for a 10× base-current overdrive (neglect $V_{CE(sat)}$).
steps.explanation:
Coil current: $I_C = V_{CC}/R_{coil}$ = {{VCC|V}} / {{Rc|Ω}} = {{IC|A}}.
Base current with 10× margin: $I_B = 10\,I_C/h_{FE}$ = 10 × {{IC|A}} / {{hFE}} = {{IB|A}}.
$R_B = (V_{in} - 0.6)/I_B$ = {{Vin-0.6|V}} / {{IB|A}} = **{{RB|Ω}}** (pick the next lower standard value).

steps.prompt: The transistor driving a relay coil switches off and there is **no** diode across the coil. What happens?
options: The coil keeps its current flowing and drives the collector far above $V_{CC}$, likely beyond the transistor's breakdown voltage
The collector is pulled to ground and the relay stays energised
The coil current stops instantly and nothing special happens
The base current reverses and the transistor switches back on
steps.explanation: An inductor resists any sudden change of current: $v = L\,di/dt$. Forcing the current to zero in a fraction of a microsecond produces hundreds of volts at the collector, exceeding $BV_{CEO}$. The flyback diode gives the current a path ($V_{CC}$ → coil → diode → $V_{CC}$), clamping the collector at $V_{CC}$ + 0.6 V while the current decays.

steps.prompt: Tap the component that keeps the transistor safely **off** while the driving logic pin is floating (e.g. during a microcontroller reset).
steps.explanation: $R_2$ from base to ground ties the base to 0 V when nothing drives $R_B$, so leakage or pickup cannot turn the transistor partly on. When the input is high it only steals a small current ($0.6\ \text{V}/R_2$) from the base drive. $D_1$ protects against the inductive kick at switch-off.

steps.prompt: A transistor switches a 12 V lamp rated {{IL|A}}. Its cold filament resistance is {{k}}× lower than when hot. With $h_{FE(min)}$ = {{hFE}}, what is the minimum base current that keeps the transistor saturated at the moment of switch-on?
steps.explanation: Cold, the lamp draws {{k}} × {{IL|A}} = {{k*IL|A}}. To stay saturated you need $I_B \ge I_C/h_{FE}$ = {{k*IL|A}} / {{hFE}} = **{{k*IL/hFE|A}}**. If the base drive were designed only for the hot current ({{IL/hFE|A}}), the transistor would come out of saturation at switch-on and dissipate a lot of power.

steps.prompt: Match each quantity with its typical value
steps.explanation: These are the numbers to carry around: one diode drop for the base–emitter junction, a few tenths of a volt or less in saturation, a wide spread in $h_{FE}$ (so never design for an exact value), a comfortable base overdrive for switches, and the large inrush current of cold filaments.

steps.title: Why followers are useful
steps.body: The output follows the input one $V_{BE}$ lower, so the voltage gain is about 1. But the base current is only $1/(h_{FE}+1)$ of the emitter current: the load looks $h_{FE}+1$ times bigger from the input, $R_{in} \approx (h_{FE}+1)(R_E \| R_L)$, and the source looks $h_{FE}+1$ times smaller from the output. Note that an npn follower can source current easily but can only sink what $R_E$ provides.

steps.prompt: An emitter follower has $R_E$ = {{RE|Ω}} and drives a load $R_L$ = {{RL|Ω}} (ac-coupled or to ground, so in parallel with $R_E$ for signals). With $h_{FE}$ = {{hFE}}, what input resistance does the signal see at the base?
steps.explanation: $R_E \| R_L$ = {{par(RE,RL)|Ω}}. Looking into the base: $R_{in} = (h_{FE}+1)(R_E \| R_L)$ = {{hFE+1}} × {{par(RE,RL)|Ω}} = **{{(hFE+1)*par(RE,RL)|Ω}}**. (A base bias divider would appear in parallel with this.)

steps.prompt: A signal source with internal resistance $R_s$ = {{Rs|Ω}} drives the base of a follower with $h_{FE}$ = {{hFE}}. Estimate the output resistance seen from the emitter (ignore $R_E$ and the transistor's own small emitter resistance).
steps.explanation: $R_{out} \approx R_s/(h_{FE}+1)$ = {{Rs|Ω}} / {{hFE+1}} = **{{Rs/(hFE+1)|Ω}}**. The follower turns a {{Rs|Ω}} source into a much stiffer one without any voltage gain.

steps.title: Biasing on a single supply
steps.body: An ac-coupled signal averages 0 V, but an npn follower on a single supply cannot drive its emitter below ground. So bias it: $V_E = V_{CC}/2$ for the largest symmetric swing, $R_E$ for the quiescent current, $V_B = V_E + 0.6$ from a stiff divider ($R_1 \| R_2 \lesssim h_{FE}R_E/10$), and coupling capacitors that pass the lowest frequency of interest.

steps.prompt: A single-supply follower ($V_{CC}$ = {{VCC|V}}) gets an ac-coupled sine of {{A|V}} peak on top of its base bias $V_B$. Set $V_B$ so that the emitter waveform is not clipped at either end.
steps.hint: The emitter swings ±{{A|V}} around its quiescent value. It cannot go below 0 V (cut-off) or above $V_{CC}$ (saturation).
steps.explanation: The emitter rests at $V_E = V_B - 0.6$ and swings ±{{A|V}}. It clips at 0 V when the transistor cuts off and near $V_{CC}$ when it saturates, so the room is largest with $V_E = V_{CC}/2$ = {{VCC/2|V}}, i.e. $V_B$ = {{VCC/2|V}} + 0.6 V = **{{VCC/2+0.6|V}}**. Any $V_E$ between {{A|V}} and {{VCC-0.2-A|V}} just avoids clipping here.

steps.prompt: You design a single-supply, ac-coupled follower with $V_{CC}$ = {{VCC|V}} and a quiescent current of {{IQ|A}}, biased for maximum symmetric swing.

ask.explanation: Maximum symmetric swing: $V_E = V_{CC}/2$ = {{VCC/2|V}}. $R_E = V_E/I_Q$ = {{VCC/2|V}} / {{IQ|A}} = **{{VCC/2/IQ|Ω}}**.

ask.prompt: What base voltage $V_B$ must the divider provide?
ask.explanation: $V_E = V_{CC}/2$ = {{VCC/2|V}}, and the base sits one diode drop higher: $V_B$ = {{VCC/2|V}} + 0.6 V = **{{VCC/2+0.6|V}}**.

steps.prompt: A follower has $R_E$ = {{RE|Ω}} and $h_{FE(min)}$ = {{hFE}}. Following the 1/10 rule, what is the largest allowed Thévenin resistance $R_1 \| R_2$ of the base divider?
steps.explanation: The dc resistance looking into the base is about $h_{FE}R_E$ = {{hFE}} × {{RE|Ω}} = {{hFE*RE|Ω}}. The divider should be 10× stiffer: $R_1 \| R_2 \le$ {{hFE*RE|Ω}} / 10 = **{{hFE*RE/10|Ω}}**. Then a change in $h_{FE}$ shifts $V_B$ only a little.

steps.prompt: An ac-coupled follower has $R_1$ = {{R1|Ω}}, $R_2$ = {{R2|Ω}}, $R_E$ = {{RE|Ω}}, $h_{FE}$ = {{hFE}} and an input capacitor $C_1$ = {{C|F}}. The load is much larger than $R_E$. Find the −3 dB corner of the input high-pass filter.
steps.explanation:
$C_1$ sees the divider in parallel with the base: $R_{in} = R_1 \| R_2 \| h_{FE}R_E$ = {{par(R1,R2)|Ω}} ∥ {{hFE*RE|Ω}} = {{Rin|Ω}}.
$f_{3dB} = 1/(2\pi R_{in}C_1)$ = 1 / (2π × {{Rin|Ω}} × {{C|F}}) = **{{1/(2*pi*Rin*C)|Hz}}**.

steps.prompt: A follower is biased by a single resistor from $V_{CC}$ to the base, calculated for $h_{FE}$ = 100. With a transistor of $h_{FE}$ = 200 the quiescent point stays about the same.
steps.explanation: With a single base resistor the base **current** is fixed, so the emitter current, and with it $V_E$, roughly doubles with $h_{FE}$ = 200, and the output may even saturate. A stiff divider fixes the base **voltage** instead; then $V_E = V_B - 0.6$ is nearly independent of $h_{FE}$.

steps.prompt: Put the design steps of a single-supply, ac-coupled emitter follower in order
items: Set the divider ratio for $V_B = V_E + 0.6$ V
Choose the coupling capacitors for the lowest frequency
steps.explanation: Start from the operating point ($V_E$, $I_Q$), which gives $R_E$. Then the divider: first its ratio (for $V_B$), then its impedance level (stiff compared with the base). The coupling capacitors come last, because they depend on the input and load impedances you just fixed.

steps.prompt: In this current source $V_{CC}$ = {{VCC|V}}; the load sits between $V_{CC}$ and the collector.

ask.explanation: $V_E = V_B - 0.6$ = {{VB-0.6|V}}, so $I \approx V_E/R_E$ = {{VB-0.6|V}} / {{RE|Ω}} = **{{I|A}}**, independent of the load (as long as the transistor is active).

ask.prompt: What is the lowest collector voltage at which it still works (the bottom of the compliance range)?
ask.explanation: The transistor must stay out of saturation: $V_C \ge V_E + 0.2$ V = {{VB-0.6|V}} + 0.2 V = **{{Vmin|V}}**.

ask.prompt: What is the largest load resistance it can drive at full current?
ask.explanation: $I$ = {{VB-0.6|V}} / {{RE|Ω}} = {{I|A}}, and the collector may drop to $V_E$ + 0.2 V = {{Vmin|V}}. So the load can take at most {{VCC|V}} − {{Vmin|V}} = {{VCC-Vmin|V}}: $R_{L,max}$ = {{VCC-Vmin|V}} / {{I|A}} = **{{(VCC-Vmin)/I|Ω}}**.

steps.prompt: A current source has $V_E$ = {{VE|V}} across its emitter resistor. The base voltage is fixed, and $V_{BE}$ drops by {{dV|V}} (e.g. warming up). By what percentage does the output current change?
steps.explanation: With $V_B$ fixed, $V_E$ rises by the full {{dV|V}}, so the current changes by $\Delta V_{BE}/V_E$ = {{dV|V}} / {{VE|V}} = **{{100*dV/VE|%}}**. That's why you keep $V_E$ at a volt or more: a few tens of mV in $V_{BE}$ then hardly matter (but a large $V_E$ costs compliance).

steps.title: The CE amplifier as two blocks
steps.body: Transconductance view: the transistor with $R_E$ is a voltage-to-current converter with $g_m = 1/R_E$; $R_C$ converts the current back to voltage. Gain $= -g_mR_C = -R_C/R_E$. To get more gain without upsetting the bias, split $R_E$ into an unbypassed $R_{E1}$ (sets the signal gain) and a part $R_{E2}$ bypassed by a capacitor (only helps the dc bias): $G \approx -R_C/R_{E1}$.

steps.prompt: For this common-emitter amplifier with $V_{CC}$ = {{VCC|V}}, assume a stiff divider (ignore the base current).

ask.prompt: Find the magnitude of the voltage gain (simple model, $G \approx -R_C/R_E$).
ask.explanation: $|G| \approx R_C/R_E$ = {{RC|Ω}} / {{RE|Ω}} = **{{RC/RE}}** (inverting).

steps.prompt: A common-emitter stage has an (unbypassed) emitter resistor $R_E$ = {{RE|Ω}}.

ask.explanation: The base wiggle appears across $R_E$, so $i_c \approx v_{in}/R_E$: $g_m = 1/R_E$ = 1 / {{RE|Ω}} = **{{1/RE|S}}**.

ask.prompt: By how much does the collector current change when the base moves by {{dv|V}}?
ask.explanation: The emitter follows the base, so $\Delta I_C \approx \Delta V_B/R_E$ = {{dv|V}} / {{RE|Ω}} = **{{dv/RE|A}}**.

steps.prompt: Design a unity-gain phase splitter on $V_{CC}$ = {{VCC|V}} with $I_Q$ = {{IQ|A}} and maximum symmetric swing at both outputs ($V_C = 0.75V_{CC}$, $V_E = 0.25V_{CC}$).

ask.explanation: $R_E = V_E/I_Q$ = {{0.25*VCC|V}} / {{IQ|A}} = **{{0.25*VCC/IQ|Ω}}**, and $R_C$ is equal (drop {{0.25*VCC|V}}, putting $V_C$ at {{0.75*VCC|V}}) for a gain of −1.
$V_B = V_E + 0.6$ = {{0.25*VCC|V}} + 0.6 V = **{{0.25*VCC+0.6|V}}**. The collector can swing from $0.5V_{CC}$ to $V_{CC}$ and the emitter from 0 to $0.5V_{CC}$: equal room for both outputs.

steps.prompt: A CE stage on $V_{CC}$ = 15 V has $R_C$ = {{RC|Ω}} and an emitter resistance made of $R_{E1}$ = {{RE1|Ω}} (unbypassed) in series with $R_{E2}$ = {{RE2|Ω}}, which is bypassed by a large capacitor. The base is held at {{VB|V}}.

ask.explanation: At dc the capacitor is open, so both resistors count: $I_C \approx (V_B - 0.6)/(R_{E1}+R_{E2})$ = {{VB-0.6|V}} / {{RE1+RE2|Ω}} = **{{(VB-0.6)/(RE1+RE2)|A}}**.

ask.prompt: Find the magnitude of the signal voltage gain (simple model).
ask.explanation: At signal frequencies $R_{E2}$ is shorted by its capacitor, so only $R_{E1}$ degenerates the stage: $|G| \approx R_C/R_{E1}$ = {{RC|Ω}} / {{RE1|Ω}} = **{{RC/RE1}}**. (The next unit adds the transistor's own $r_e$ to $R_{E1}$.)

steps.prompt: A CE amplifier has $R_1$ = {{R1|Ω}}, $R_2$ = {{R2|Ω}}, an unbypassed $R_E$ = {{RE|Ω}} and $h_{FE}$ = 100. What input resistance does the signal source see (coupling capacitor a short)?
steps.explanation: The source sees three paths in parallel: $R_1$ (to $V_{CC}$, an ac ground), $R_2$, and the base, which looks like $h_{FE}R_E$ = {{100*RE|Ω}}. $R_{in} = R_1 \| R_2 \| h_{FE}R_E$ = **{{par(R1,R2,100*RE)|Ω}}**. Forgetting the factor $h_{FE}$ or the divider are the usual mistakes.

steps.prompt: The output impedance of a common-emitter amplifier is approximately $R_C$.
steps.explanation: Looking into the collector you see a (poor but decent) current source: an impedance of megohms. In parallel with $R_C$ that leaves about $R_C$. The emitter of a follower, by contrast, is a low-impedance point.

steps.prompt: Design a degenerated CE amplifier with $V_{CC}$ = {{VCC|V}}, gain −{{G}} and $I_Q$ = {{IQ|A}}, with the collector at $V_{CC}/2$.

ask.explanation: Half the supply across $R_C$: $R_C = (V_{CC}/2)/I_Q$ = {{VCC/2|V}} / {{IQ|A}} = **{{RC|Ω}}**.

$R_C$ = {{RC|Ω}}, $R_E = R_C/{{G}}$ = {{RE|Ω}}, so $V_E = I_QR_E$ = {{IQ*RE|V}} and $V_B = V_E + 0.6$ = **{{IQ*RE+0.6|V}}**. With $V_E \ge$ 1 V the bias is insensitive to $V_{BE}$ drift; for much higher gains $V_E$ would get too small (see the next unit).

steps.prompt: A base divider from $V_{CC}$ = {{VCC|V}} must deliver $V_B$ = {{VB|V}} with a Thévenin resistance $R_1 \| R_2$ = {{Rth|Ω}} ($R_1$ to $V_{CC}$, $R_2$ to ground).

ask.explanation: Similarly $R_{th} = R_2(V_{CC} - V_B)/V_{CC}$, so $R_2 = R_{th}V_{CC}/(V_{CC} - V_B)$ = {{Rth|Ω}} × {{VCC|V}} / {{VCC-VB|V}} = **{{Rth*VCC/(VCC-VB)|Ω}}**. Check: {{Rth*VCC/VB|Ω}} ∥ {{Rth*VCC/(VCC-VB)|Ω}} = {{Rth|Ω}}.

steps.prompt: The stage has a divider with $R_1 \| R_2$ = {{Rth|Ω}}, an unbypassed $R_E$ = {{RE|Ω}} and $h_{FE}$ = {{hFE}}. Choose the input coupling capacitor that puts the −3 dB corner at {{f|Hz}}.
steps.explanation:
$R_{in} = R_1 \| R_2 \| h_{FE}R_E$ = {{Rth|Ω}} ∥ {{hFE*RE|Ω}} = {{Rin|Ω}}.
$C = 1/(2\pi f R_{in})$ = 1 / (2π × {{f|Hz}} × {{Rin|Ω}}) = **{{1/(2*pi*f*Rin)|F}}**. Round up to a standard value.

steps.prompt: A relay coil with $L$ = {{L|H}} and $R$ = {{Rc|Ω}} runs from {{VCC|V}}.

ask.prompt: Without a flyback diode, the transistor turns off in about 1 µs. Estimate the induced voltage $L\,\Delta I/\Delta t$.
ask.explanation: Coil current $I = V_{CC}/R$ = {{I|A}}. $v = L\,\Delta I/\Delta t$ = {{L|H}} × {{I|A}} / 1 µs = **{{L*I/1e-6|V}}**. In reality the collector breaks down long before, which is why the diode is mandatory.

ask.prompt: With the flyback diode (drop neglected), how fast does the coil current decay? Give the time constant.
ask.explanation: The current circulates through coil and diode and decays with $\tau = L/R$ = {{L|H}} / {{Rc|Ω}} = **{{L/Rc|s}}**. Side effect: the relay releases more slowly. A zener in series with the diode speeds this up.

steps.prompt: A split-supply follower ($\pm${{VEE|V}}) has $R_E$ = {{RE|Ω}} to $-V_{EE}$ and drives $R_L$ = {{RL|Ω}} to ground; the output rests at 0 V. What is the largest sine **amplitude** it can deliver without clipping?
steps.explanation: Positive swings are easy: the transistor sources the current. On negative swings the load current must flow through $R_E$; at cut-off the output is the divider $-V_{EE}R_L/(R_L+R_E)$ = −{{VEE|V}} × {{RL|Ω}} / {{RL+RE|Ω}} = −{{Vm|V}}. So the clean amplitude is limited to **{{Vm|V}}**.

steps.prompt: The follower in the previous question clips its negative peaks. Which change cures it (keeping the same load)?
options: Decrease $R_E$, so the quiescent current is at least the peak load current
Drive the base harder from a lower-impedance source
steps.explanation: An npn follower cannot sink current; on negative peaks only $R_E$ can pull the output down. Lowering $R_E$ raises the quiescent current so that it covers the peak load current (at the cost of more dissipation), or you replace $R_E$ by a current sink, or use a push-pull stage. The base drive is not the problem: the transistor is simply cut off.

steps.prompt: A single-supply follower on $V_{CC}$ = 12 V is biased at $V_E$ = 3.6 V instead of 6 V, and gets an ac-coupled sine of 4.8 V peak. Which graph shows $v_E$?
steps.explanation: The emitter swings from 3.6 − 4.8 = −1.2 V to 3.6 + 4.8 = 8.4 V. It cannot go below 0 V (the transistor cuts off), so the **bottoms** are flattened at 0 V while the tops are fine. Biased at 6 V the same signal would fit with 1.2 V to spare.
